title: UK Households Urged to Prepare for Extreme Weather and Possible Food Supply Disruptions
summary: People across the UK are being encouraged to take practical steps to prepare for possible disruption to food supplies as concerns grow about extreme weather, cyber-attacks and other threats to the country's supply chains. The advice comes as the government prepares to publish a new national emergency preparedness strategy later in 2026. The strategy is expected to explain some of the simple measures households can take to cope with shortages of essential goods and services during emergencies.
body_markdown:
People across the UK are being encouraged to take practical steps to prepare for possible disruption to food supplies as concerns grow about extreme weather, cyber-attacks and other threats to the country's supply chains.


The advice comes as the government prepares to publish a new national emergency preparedness strategy later in 2026. The strategy is expected to explain some of the simple measures households can take to cope with shortages of essential goods and services during emergencies.


Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle has urged households to consider keeping a modest supply of food at home. Her comments come amid warnings that a particularly powerful El Niño weather pattern is developing in the Pacific Ocean and could contribute to more unusual weather conditions around the world.


## What is behind the warning?


El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern involving changes in ocean temperatures and atmospheric conditions in the Pacific. Although its strongest effects are often felt in regions around the Pacific, it can influence weather patterns much farther away.


According to the comments reported by the BBC and other media outlets, Dame Angela Eagle warned that the developing El Niño could be associated with drier summers, wetter winters and more severe storms in the UK.


The potential consequences are not limited to the weather itself. Severe storms, flooding and other extreme events can affect roads, ports, warehouses, farms and distribution networks. When these systems are disrupted, getting food from producers to supermarkets can become more difficult.


That does not necessarily mean Britain is facing an imminent food shortage. Instead, the warnings highlight the importance of being prepared for temporary interruptions.


A small household supply could be useful if deliveries are delayed, shops are temporarily inaccessible or people are advised to remain at home during a serious weather event.


## Food supply chains face several risks


The warning about household preparedness is also linked to a broader report from the National Audit Office.


The NAO highlighted several threats to Britain's food supply system, including extreme weather, plant and animal diseases, human disease outbreaks and cyber-attacks.


Modern food distribution relies on a complex network of farmers, manufacturers, transport companies, warehouses, supermarkets and technology systems. Problems in one part of that network can sometimes have consequences elsewhere.


For example, a major cyber incident affecting an important company could interfere with ordering, payments, logistics or deliveries. Severe weather could make roads difficult to use or temporarily prevent goods from being transported.


The report also identified climate change as a longer-term concern. Changing environmental conditions can affect agricultural production and increase pressure on food systems.


If disruptions become severe enough, they could also contribute to higher food prices. That could be particularly difficult for households that are already struggling with the cost of essential goods.


## Should households start panic buying?


The advice being discussed by officials should not be confused with a recommendation to panic buy.


There is an important difference between sensible preparation and buying large quantities of products unnecessarily.


Keeping a reasonable amount of long-lasting food at home can provide some additional security during an emergency. However, emptying supermarket shelves or purchasing far more than a household needs could create additional pressure on supply chains.


A practical approach is to gradually build a small emergency supply while continuing to shop normally.


Items with a relatively long shelf life can include canned vegetables, beans, soups, rice, pasta, cereals, dried foods and other household staples. Bottled or otherwise safely stored drinking water can also be useful in circumstances where the normal water supply is temporarily affected.


Households should consider what they actually use rather than buying products simply because they are being promoted as emergency supplies.


## Why emergency preparation matters


The UK's food system has generally continued operating through major disruptions in recent years. However, recent events have demonstrated how quickly unexpected problems can affect everyday life.


Extreme weather can cause flooding and transport difficulties. Global events can interfere with shipping and international trade. Disease outbreaks can affect agricultural production, while cyber incidents can target businesses and infrastructure.


The National Audit Office has suggested that UK households are less prepared for emergencies than people in some other countries, including Finland and Sweden.


Several European countries have placed greater emphasis on household preparedness, encouraging residents to maintain supplies that can help them cope if normal services are temporarily interrupted.


The UK government has indicated that it wants to encourage similar levels of preparedness.


## What could households realistically keep at home?


Emergency preparation does not have to be complicated or expensive.


One sensible option is to maintain a rotating supply of foods that the household already eats. When a new product is purchased, an older item can be used first. This helps prevent food waste while gradually maintaining a useful reserve.


A basic household supply might include:


- Tinned vegetables and fruit
- Beans and pulses
- Rice and pasta
- Cereal and other breakfast foods
- Long-life milk or suitable alternatives
- Crackers and other long-lasting foods
- Cooking ingredients such as oil, salt and basic seasonings
- Pet food where necessary
- Drinking water
- Essential household and hygiene products


People with specific dietary requirements should also consider keeping suitable alternatives that they can safely store.


The goal is not to transform an ordinary home into a warehouse. Instead, it is about having enough basic supplies to make a temporary disruption easier to manage.


## The role of supermarkets and businesses


Household preparation is only one part of the issue.


The National Audit Office has raised concerns about how responsibility for dealing with food supply disruptions is divided between the government and private businesses.


Supermarkets and food companies play a central role in keeping products moving around the country. However, the report suggests that government planning also needs to account for situations in which businesses themselves are affected by major disruptions.


Phil Pluck, chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, has also warned about vulnerabilities within Britain's food distribution network.


Temperature-controlled transport is particularly important for products such as meat, dairy and some fresh foods. Any serious interruption to refrigeration, transportation or distribution could therefore create additional challenges.


He has argued that households should maintain sensible supplies rather than relying entirely on supermarkets and other businesses during every possible emergency.


## What happens next?


The government has said it plans to provide households with more information about preparing for emergencies.


Plans announced earlier in 2026 are expected to include guidance covering potential food and water shortages caused by extreme weather, cyber-attacks and other emergencies.


A wider strategy is due to be published before the end of the year.


The objective is expected to be greater national resilience, with households, businesses and public authorities all playing a role.


For households, the message is relatively straightforward. Preparation does not necessarily require major spending or dramatic changes to everyday life. Keeping a modest amount of useful food and essential supplies available can provide an additional safety net if normal services are temporarily disrupted.


## A sensible approach to preparedness


The latest warnings serve as a reminder that food availability depends on a much larger system than what consumers see on supermarket shelves.


Farmers, manufacturers, warehouses, transport networks, ports, technology systems and retailers all have to work together for food to reach homes.


Extreme weather and other emergencies can put pressure on different parts of that system at the same time.


That is why officials are encouraging people to think about resilience before a crisis occurs rather than waiting until supermarket shelves are affected.


For most households, the most sensible response is likely to be gradual and proportionate. Buying a little extra of food that is already regularly consumed, keeping essential supplies organised and paying attention to official emergency advice can all help.


There is no need for panic buying. The purpose of household preparedness is simply to make families less dependent on immediate access to shops if an unexpected disruption occurs.


As the UK prepares for potentially more challenging weather patterns and continues to assess risks to its food supply network, a small amount of planning could make temporary disruptions easier to manage.


### Source


BBC News report published on 4 September 2026, together with the National Audit Office findings and comments from government and industry representatives.
